extracted.intended_audience: prose writers (essayists, bloggers, fiction writers) seeking practical techniques to make writing funny
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance and micro-rubrics for adding humor to sentences and paragraphs in prose (essays, blog posts, short fiction). Focuses on levers like specificity, surprise, sound, voice, and paragraph-level structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specificity
rubrics_metrics.description: "a Honda Civic" beats "a car."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer concrete, specific nouns and details rather than generic terms. Specificity grounds the image and makes the incongruity or absurdity sharper and funnier. Example: use 'a Honda Civic' instead of 'a car.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Surprise (punchline placement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the unexpected word at the end of the sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: End sentences or paragraphs with the surprising or funniest word — bury the twist so the reader's expectations are subverted at the last moment. Also applies at paragraph-level: open with surprise and bury the punchline at the end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sound
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentences with consonant clusters and rhythm scan funnier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pay attention to phonetics and rhythm: hard consonants, alliteration, consonant clusters and sentence cadence can increase comic effect. Example techniques: k-sound rule, deliberate consonant choices, musical rhythm in sentence construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-awareness (comic voice)
rubrics_metrics.description: The writer's voice noticing what's absurd.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a voice that recognizes absurdity without over-explaining or begging for laughs. Self-aware narration that comments on a situation can create distance and comedic perspective. Avoid making yourself the heroic center of the funny story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stakes (incongruous valuation)
rubrics_metrics.description: What would normally be tragic, played as banal (or vice versa).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flip expected stakes or treat serious events as trivial (understatement) or trivial events as gravely important (inflation) to create humor. This is closely tied to tonal whiplash and the understated noun technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: K-sound rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Words containing K (kale, Kafka, Kalamazoo) are funnier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose words with hard K sounds to boost comedic impact; examples provided include kale, Kafka, Kalamazoo. Use this as a playful phonetic tool rather than a formulaic crutch.

rubrics_metrics.name: List-of-three with absurd third
rubrics_metrics.description: The list-of-three with the absurd third: 'He brought wine, cheese, and his ex-wife.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use two plausible items followed by an unexpected, absurd, or hyper-specific third item to create comedic escalation. Rhythm and expectation set-up are key.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unexpectedly precise number
rubrics_metrics.description: Not 'a lot of' but '31.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replace vague quantifiers with oddly precise numbers to create specificity and surprise. The arbitrary precision can read as observational detail and be funny because it's oddly exact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tonal whiplash (register-shift)
rubrics_metrics.description: An academic register collapses into colloquial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abrupt shifts in register (e.g., lofty/academic language suddenly switching to colloquial or crude language) create surprise and comedy. Use sparingly to avoid feeling jarring rather than funny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understated noun
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy described as 'an inconvenience.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe high-stakes or dramatic events with diminutive or neutral nouns to produce a deadpan, comic understatement. Works well with self-awareness and low-key tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open with the most surprising sentence
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin a paragraph with a sentence that surprises the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lead paragraphs with unexpected or strong lines to hook the reader and establish a comedic beat. This sets context for the rest of the paragraph and primes the punchline placement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bury the punchline at the end of the paragraph
rubrics_metrics.description: Place the joke or twist at the paragraph's end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure paragraphs so that the setup comes first and the surprise punchline comes last, maximizing the impact of the reveal when the reader reaches the end of the paragraph.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use callbacks across paragraphs
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a callback in the next paragraph to the previous joke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer back to earlier jokes or lines in subsequent paragraphs to build cumulative humor and reward attentive readers. Callbacks create a sense of coherence and escalating comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short, staccato paragraphs
rubrics_metrics.description: Short paragraphs. Then. Sometimes. Even shorter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use very short sentences and paragraphs (fragmentation) for comedic timing and punch. Pauses and abrupt stops can mimic timing effects from spoken comedy; vary length for rhythm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't tell the reader something is funny
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid words like 'hilariously' or 'comically.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show, don't tell: don't label text as funny — let the humor arise from phrasing and observation. Calling something 'hilarious' undercuts the reader's discovery and feels like forcing laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid exclamation points
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclamation points!!!
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refrain from overusing exclamation points to force emphasis or laughs; they often read as pleading for reaction rather than eliciting genuine humor. Let word choice and structure carry the emphasis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid italics for emphasis
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't use italics for emphasis instead of better word choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on diction, placement, and sentence shape for emphasis rather than typographic shortcuts like italics, which can feel lazy or manipulative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't make yourself the hero of the funny story
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid centering yourself as the triumphant or clever protagonist in humorous anecdotes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Self-deprecating perspective or observational stance often works better than portraying oneself as the comedic victor; making yourself the hero can alienate readers or feel boastful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't quote your own clever line earlier
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid quoting your own clever line earlier in the piece.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't pre-announce or reprint your punchline; repeating or spotlighting your own witty line reduces its impact and feels like you are selling the joke rather than letting it land naturally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Is there one specific, concrete noun? (sentence test)
rubrics_metrics.description: Check whether the sentence contains a single specific, concrete noun.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A strong funny sentence often hinges on one concrete noun that anchors the image; use this as a quick litmus test when editing sentences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Does the sentence end on the funniest word? (sentence test)
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the sentence end on the funniest word?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the terminal word of the sentence delivers the punch or twist; if not, rearrange so the surprise sits at the end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Does it use a hard consonant or unexpected register-shift? (sentence test)
rubrics_metrics.description: Does it use a hard consonant or unexpected register-shift?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for phonetic punch (hard consonants like K) or an abrupt shift in tone/register within the sentence; either can increase comedic payoff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Could the sentence stand alone in a tweet and get a laugh? (sentence test)
rubrics_metrics.description: Could the sentence stand alone in a tweet and get a laugh?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the sentence works as an isolated unit and still evokes laughter, it's likely tightly constructed and effective as a comic line.

rubrics_metrics.name: Is the tone deadpan rather than nudging? (sentence test)
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the tone deadpan rather than nudging?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer a deadpan delivery that lets the reader discover the humor, instead of 'nudging' the reader with overt signals (e.g., winking asides, punctuation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Does it earn the laugh through observation, not insistence? (sentence test)
rubrics_metrics.description: Does it earn the laugh through observation, not insistence?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good comic lines arise from sharp observation and precise phrasing; avoid forcing the joke via meta-comments, stage directions, or pleading for the reader's reaction.
